claims.summary: A key object — Key objects support cryptographic operations such as encryption and signing. They are appropriate when the application needs those operations, rather than retrieval of an opaque provider-issued token.

A secret object — Store the token as a Key Vault secret. Choose the object type by the operation the application needs. Secret retrieval returns an opaque value; key operations and certificate lifecycle management solve different requirements. This does not make every authentication token a cryptographic key object.
A certificate object — Certificate objects manage X.509 certificates and their lifecycle. They fit certificate issuance or renewal requirements, not this provider-issued token string.

Call get_secret for each discovered secret name. — get_secret retrieves a KeyVaultSecret including its value. It is useful for an application that must use a credential, but it violates this metadata-only retrieval design.

Call list_properties_of_secret_versions for one secret name. — This operation inventories the versions of a particular named secret. It suits rotation-history analysis, not discovery of the separate secret names throughout this vault.

Call list_properties_of_secrets for the vault. — Use list_properties_of_secrets for metadata-only discovery. The distinction is both scope and returned information: listing secrets discovers named objects, listing versions inspects one object's history, and getting a secret retrieves its value. Metadata visibility is not proof that an identity can read secret values.

Key Vault Secrets User — Assign Key Vault Secrets User to the application's managed identity. Successful Microsoft Entra authentication does not by itself authorize secret access. The requirement excludes both metadata-only access and secret-management privileges. Scope the role assignment to the intended vault rather than expanding unrelated resource access.
Key Vault Reader — Reader exposes metadata without revealing secret values. It is appropriate for discovery tools, but not a service that must retrieve the credential value.
Key Vault Secrets Officer — Secrets Officer grants secret-management operations in addition to access. It suits rotation operators, but exceeds the explicitly read-only requirement.
Key Vault Contributor — Contributor manages the vault resource's control plane rather than granting secret data-plane reads. It suits vault administration, not runtime credential retrieval.

Publish B in Key Vault and restart the application to reload its configuration. — The unit documents manual publication followed by restart as a rotation strategy. That fits an application whose operational plan permits restart; it does not provide the required uninterrupted transition for these long-running replicas.

Use a near-expiry event to publish B in Key Vault, leaving consumer refresh to its normal schedule. — Near-expiry automation is a documented way to initiate credential replacement before expiry. Publishing a replacement alone does not establish which replicas use it or define when A can be retired; the question needs that consumer-adoption boundary.

Publish B in Key Vault, confirm each replica is using B, and then revoke A at the provider. — Retain A until every replica has adopted B, then retire A at the provider. Key Vault publication and consumer adoption are separate steps. The stipulated provider permits overlap, so confirmation of adoption supplies the safe boundary for retiring the credential cached by existing replicas. This does not claim that storing a secret changes credentials in the external service or refreshes every client automatically.

Set enabled=False on the targeted version with update_secret_properties(). — Disable the specific version to prevent subsequent retrieval through Key Vault. The versioning unit explicitly distinguishes informational expiration from the enabled property. Updating version properties is different from deleting the secret or revoking credentials already held by downstream clients. No claim about not-before semantics is needed.

Set an earlier expires_on timestamp on the targeted version. — Expiration records intended credential lifetime and supports lifecycle monitoring. The unit explicitly says expired secrets remain retrievable; moving that timestamp does not supply this access block.

Add a rotation-policy tag to the targeted version. — Tags support organization and rotation-policy reporting. They can document a policy but are metadata, not the enabled property that controls retrieval of this version.

Preload the secret once per process and retain it until that process restarts. — Startup-only caching minimizes reads for secrets that remain unchanged during a process lifetime. Long-lived replicas can exceed the explicit five-minute staleness bound, so that cache lifetime is unsuitable here.

Cache the secret in each process and refetch on access once its five-minute TTL expires. — Use a time-bounded in-memory cache per process. The design balances two independent constraints: bounded local age and no new shared secret store. It does not promise that a timer alone refreshes an idle or disconnected process. A fleet still needs throttling-aware retries and load management; a TTL is not proof that all failures are impossible.

Place the secret in a shared cache and have one worker refresh it every five minutes. — A shared cache can reduce fleet-wide vault reads, but stores credentials in another service that requires its own protection. It would fit a policy allowing that additional storage, which this stem forbids.

SecretNearExpiry — Near-expiry notification can initiate rotation before a credential ages out. It does not specifically identify that a replacement version has just been stored, which is the invalidation trigger required here.

SecretExpired — Expiration notification supports lifecycle monitoring at expiry. It is appropriate for expired-secret handling, but can occur independently of creating a replacement and needlessly delays adoption.

SecretNewVersionCreated — Invalidate the entry on SecretNewVersionCreated. An event about creating a new version directly matches the cache-change trigger. Invalidation is application behavior; the event does not itself update every in-memory copy. Keeping time-based expiration avoids making cache freshness depend exclusively on successful notification delivery.

Keep both as direct App Configuration values. — Direct values fit non-sensitive operational settings, such as the retry count. The access-granting token instead belongs in Key Vault; treating both as ordinary settings misses the requested secret-storage boundary.

Keep the retry count in App Configuration and reference a Key Vault token. — Store the retry count directly in App Configuration and the token in Key Vault, exposed through a reference. Placement follows sensitivity and lifecycle rather than whether both values are strings. A reference does not copy the token into App Configuration. This answer assumes the provider is configured to resolve references; it does not imply that access to the configuration store authorizes secret retrieval.

Keep both in Key Vault and reference both from App Configuration. — References can provide a unified reading path for secret values. This placement could fit two sensitive values, but placing the non-sensitive retry count in Key Vault violates the policy reserving the vault for sensitive data.

config["RetryPolicy"]["attempts"] — Read the nested mapping with config["RetryPolicy"]["attempts"]. The application/json content type causes the provider to interpret RetryPolicy as a JSON object. The loaded provider Mapping then exposes that object under the literal RetryPolicy key. A colon in another key name would be a key-naming convention, not an automatic nested-JSON lookup.

config["RetryPolicy:attempts"] — A colon can be part of a literal hierarchical setting key. This expression would fit a separately stored key named RetryPolicy:attempts, which the stem does not define; it is not nested JSON-property access.
config["attempts"] — This looks up a top-level setting named attempts. It would work if that independent key were loaded, but the provided attempts value is a property inside RetryPolicy.

Use separate keys 'Classifier:Threshold:Development' and 'Classifier:Threshold:Production'. — Separate hierarchical key names are a valid organization pattern when applications choose different lookup keys. They do not preserve this common application key without an additional transformation.

Use one null-labeled 'Classifier:Threshold' setting as the shared default. — A single null-labeled value is the documented shared-default pattern. It fits deployments that can use the same threshold; it cannot represent both of the stipulated different values.

Use key 'Classifier:Threshold' with Development and Production labels. — Represent the environments with labels on the same key. The key stays stable and the selected label chooses the variant. A null label is itself a variant used for defaults, not an instruction to load every environment. This question concerns identity of stored settings, not precedence when several selectors are composed.

Keep the existing selector order and remove the Production BatchSize setting. — Removing the override leaves the default BatchSize=20, which is useful when all environments should share the default. It cannot produce the required Production value of 80.

Load the null-label selector first and the Production selector second. — Load defaults first, then apply the Production overlay. Selector composition is ordered rather than an automatic preference for a label named Production. Reversing the order simultaneously corrects the override and retains an inherited default. Selecting only the environment would discard a needed value.

Load only the Production selector and omit the null-label selector. — Selecting only Production obtains its BatchSize override but does not load the missing Timeout default. It fits a fully populated environment label, not this sparse override set.

Select key filter 'AuditWorker:*' and label Production; trim prefix 'AuditWorker:'. — Use both a scoped key/label selector and a local prefix trim. Filtering and trimming act on different parts of the loading process. Prefix trimming is neither an authorization mechanism nor a filter; selectors also do not rename keys. No store mutation is needed for the requested local mapping.

Select key filter '*' and label Production; trim prefix 'AuditWorker:'. — Trimming removes a prefix from matching loaded names but does not exclude other applications' keys. This wider selector suits an application needing all Production settings, which the stem excludes.

Select key filter 'AuditWorker:*' and label Production; leave prefixes untrimmed. — The selector correctly limits loaded settings, but preserves AuditWorker:BatchSize as the local key. It fits code using fully qualified keys, not the required BatchSize lookup.

Change the sentinel, write the first setting, then write the second setting. — Updating the sentinel first can cause a worker to reload before both writes finish. A sentinel may be updated alone when the desired settings are already complete, but that precondition is absent here.

Write the first setting, change the sentinel, then write the second setting. — This signals a reload while the second value is still old. It would fit a release consisting only of the first setting, not this paired update.

Write both settings, then change the sentinel for the completed release. — Publish both setting changes before updating the sentinel. Update the sentinel after the related writes have completed. This is a publication-order rule for the specified watcher pattern, not a cross-key transaction, a rollback mechanism or a guarantee about concurrent publishers. A worker can retain the preceding configuration until its next eligible explicit refresh.

App Configuration Data Reader at the configuration store — Assign App Configuration Data Reader and Key Vault Secrets User to the application identity at their respective resources. App Configuration stores a URI reference rather than a copy of the value. Successful reading of that URI does not authorize the provider's subsequent vault access. A single identity can authenticate to both services, but each service still requires its own authorization.

Key Vault Reader at the referenced vault — Key Vault Reader permits metadata discovery, not reading the referenced secret value. It suits inventory, but cannot replace the secret-value permission needed by reference resolution.

App Configuration Data Owner at the configuration store — Data Owner includes modifying settings and is suitable for operators or publishing pipelines. It exceeds the explicit read-only data-access requirement and is not the least-privilege choice here.

Key Vault Secrets User at the referenced vault — Assign App Configuration Data Reader and Key Vault Secrets User to the application identity at their respective resources. App Configuration stores a URI reference rather than a copy of the value. Successful reading of that URI does not authorize the provider's subsequent vault access. A single identity can authenticate to both services, but each service still requires its own authorization.

Add trim_prefixes for the ordinary application-setting prefix. — Prefix trimming adjusts local setting names. It is useful for simplifying lookups, but does not enable the independent feature-flag refresh mechanism.

Set feature_flag_refresh_enabled to true. — Enable feature_flag_refresh_enabled. Flag loading, flag evaluation, ordinary-setting refresh and feature-flag refresh are distinct steps. The shown setup loads flags but does not enable their refresh. feature_flag_refresh_enabled=True adds that path; the existing refresh calls still matter.

Add another ordinary setting to refresh_on. — Watching an additional setting can trigger regular-configuration reloads. It is appropriate when that setting signals ordinary changes, but it does not substitute for independently enabling flag refresh.

Assign both services the same service.name resource attribute. — With no namespace configured, a common service.name represents one logical service, such as several replicas; with a namespace, role naming includes both attributes. Neither naming strategy transports the caller’s trace and parent-span IDs across HTTP.

Preserve traceparent and let the receiver extract the propagated context. — Restore trace-context propagation through the proxy. Exporter delivery, resource naming, and context propagation are separate concerns. Both services can report valid telemetry while their traces remain disconnected. The requested relationship depends on transmitting and consuming the calling span's context.

Configure a distinct service.instance.id for each running process. — service.instance.id identifies a running instance for replica diagnostics. It does not convey a trace’s parent context on an incoming call.

An instrumentation library — Instrumentation libraries observe framework or library operations and produce telemetry. They suit capturing an HTTP call or database operation, rather than selecting the backend transport.

The OpenTelemetry API surface — The APIs define interfaces used by instrumentation to describe telemetry. They permit vendor-neutral authoring but are not the backend-specific serialization and transport implementation.

The Azure Monitor exporter — The Azure Monitor exporter performs that serialization and transmission. The API, SDK, instrumentation, and exporter work together but do not have interchangeable responsibilities. Changing the export destination need not require rewriting every vendor-neutral span declaration, although backend capabilities and configuration can differ.

Import and call configure_azure_monitor once during startup. — Call configure_azure_monitor during startup. The prerequisites in the stem separate package installation and destination configuration from actual initialization. Custom instrumentation can then use the configured global providers. This does not claim every Python framework or third-party library is instrumented automatically.

Obtain a tracer with trace.get_tracer and begin application work. — get_tracer obtains an instrumentation source after provider configuration. It is appropriate for creating custom spans in an initialized application but is not a replacement for the missing distro setup.

Set OTEL_SERVICE_NAME and begin application work. — OTEL_SERVICE_NAME supplies resource identity when telemetry is configured. It is useful for naming a service but does not itself initialize the Python distro or exporter.

Set OTEL_SERVICE_NAME to the live resource's display name. — The service name changes cloud-role identity, not the ingestion resource. It is appropriate for map naming but cannot override the explicit connection_string value.

Remove the connection_string argument and use configure_azure_monitor(). — Remove the explicit archive connection string so the standard environment variable can determine the destination. The supplied argument is not a fallback: code wins over the environment for connection-string selection. A connection string identifies where telemetry is sent; this explanation does not equate it with secret-read permissions or authorization to query telemetry.

Set service.instance.id to a new value for each process. — Instance identity distinguishes processes at the same telemetry destination. It is useful for replica diagnostics but does not select an ingestion endpoint.

Use the replica ID as service.name and omit service.instance.id. — service.name defines cloud-role identity, so a distinct replica name creates distinct logical roles. It suits treating each process as a separate component, not the requested two service nodes.

Use one shared service.name for both services and distinct service.instance.id values. — Instance IDs distinguish processes but the common role name does not separate API from worker. This fits replicas of one logical service rather than two different services.

Use one service.name per logical service and distinct service.instance.id values per replica. — Keep service.name stable within each service and vary service.instance.id by replica. Logical topology and deployment-instance identity answer different diagnostic questions. Neither resource attribute replaces distributed trace context, and choosing different values does not require different Application Insights resources.

A SERVER span handling an incoming HTTP request — SERVER and CONSUMER spans map to requests. CLIENT, INTERNAL, and PRODUCER spans map to dependencies in this Application Insights query scope. The choice of kind should describe the operation, not simply force a preferred visualization. The traces table is for log records, not a catch-all table for distributed spans.

An INTERNAL span timing a local calculation — INTERNAL is appropriate for local computation, but maps to dependencies, including the default custom InProc span. It is not one of the requested request-table operations.

A PRODUCER span sending an asynchronous message — PRODUCER fits initiating asynchronous work, but maps to dependencies. It would be correct when selecting outgoing/asynchronous-production operations, not this table set.

A CONSUMER span processing an asynchronous message — SERVER and CONSUMER spans map to requests. CLIENT, INTERNAL, and PRODUCER spans map to dependencies in this Application Insights query scope. The choice of kind should describe the operation, not simply force a preferred visualization. The traces table is for log records, not a catch-all table for distributed spans.

span.set_attribute("validation.outcome", "failed") — An attribute provides custom per-operation context and can be queried later. It is useful for recording business outcomes, but does not replace the span’s status field.

span.set_status(Status(StatusCode.ERROR, "Validation failed")) — Set the span status to ERROR; the exception details are already recorded. Recording an exception and classifying an operation’s status are separate actions. Because the handler catches the exception inside the span and continues, an exception escaping the context manager is not the mechanism being used. An explicit ERROR status represents this failed operation.

span.set_status(Status(StatusCode.OK)) — OK explicitly classifies an operation as successful and is appropriate after successful work. Continuing program execution does not mean the stipulated validation operation succeeded.

Disable trace-based log sampling with enable_trace_based_sampling_for_logs=False. — Disable the log filter that follows a trace’s sampled flag while leaving the trace sampler unchanged. The documented log rule uses valid span context and the trace sampling flag. Opting out permits logs associated with unsampled traces to pass this rule; it does not change the trace sampling policy, recreate missing spans or override other logging filters.

Set fixed-percentage trace sampling to sampling_ratio=1.0. — A ratio of 1.0 is appropriate when the goal is to retain all traces rather than a fraction. It changes the trace population, which this diagnostic window explicitly needs to preserve.

Enable trace-based log sampling with enable_trace_based_sampling_for_logs=True. — Enabling the rule aligns logs with sampled traces and suppresses correlated logs from unsampled traces. It fits a cost/consistency policy, but conflicts with the diagnostic requirement here.

Set storage_directory to the writable directory and keep offline storage enabled. — Override storage_directory with the approved writable location while retaining offline storage. Offline persistence is resilience against temporary connectivity loss, not a durable audit guarantee. The documentation describes retries for up to 48 hours and possible drops when time or size limits are exceeded. Directory selection does not remove those bounds.

Set disable_offline_storage to true and leave the default directory unchanged. — Disabling storage is a documented option when local telemetry persistence is unwanted. It avoids use of a directory but gives up the buffering capability the team requests.

Reduce the trace sampling ratio and leave the unwritable directory unchanged. — Lower sampling can reduce telemetry volume and ingestion cost. It can help capacity pressure, but cannot make an unwritable offline-storage location usable.
requests — requests is the Application Insights resource-scoped table name. It is appropriate when opening that resource's query scope, rather than the workspace schema explicitly used here.

AppRequests — Use AppRequests in the workspace query scope. Query scope affects table and column naming. Switching between Application Insights and its workspace requires checking the complete schema, not blindly copying a query or substituting a table name while keeping incompatible columns.
AppDependencies — AppDependencies contains outbound dependency telemetry in the workspace schema. It is appropriate for downstream calls, not incoming request records.
AppExceptions — AppExceptions is the workspace table for exceptions. It suits error-detail investigation rather than the full set of incoming request records.

Move the timestamp where clause before summarize. — Filter by timestamp before aggregating. A KQL pipeline passes each operator's output to the next. The summarized result contains grouping columns and aggregates, not every original column. Adding timestamp as a grouping key changes the result's granularity instead of preserving the intended total.

Add timestamp to the summarize grouping and leave where last. — Grouping by timestamp retains a timestamp column, but splits each service across distinct event timestamps. That fits per-timestamp results rather than a single two-hour total per service.

Remove the timestamp where clause and retain summarize. — This produces one count per service across all input data. It is suitable for an unrestricted input population, not the explicitly required last-two-hour window.

Replace the final summarize with project name, model. — A projection of name and model is valid for inspecting each retained row’s descriptive fields. It does not calculate the required percentile and avoids rather than repairs the missing duration input.

Change the final aggregation to summarize retainedRows = count() by model. — Counting retained rows is a valid volume analysis and does not need duration. It changes the requested statistic instead of preserving the latency calculation.

Change the earlier projection to project name, model, duration. — Include duration in the projected columns. The defect is column lifetime, not percentile syntax or the JSON-derived model. project can itself calculate columns, but only its selected outputs continue through the pipeline. The repair preserves the intended statistic and grouping rather than making the error disappear by changing the question.
Two groups: web=5 and worker=4. — Those totals would follow grouping only by cloud_RoleName. The actual query also groups by resultCode, so web's two result codes remain separate.

Three groups: web/200=3, web/500=2, and worker/200=4. — It returns one row per role/result-code combination: counts 3, 2, and 4. The full by clause defines granularity, not only its first column. The scenario deliberately counts retained rows with one event per row; it does not claim count() compensates for telemetry sampling.

Nine groups: one row with count 1 for each request. — Per-request output would require a unique request grouping key or no grouping aggregation. Repeated role/result combinations collapse into shared groups in this query.

Filter six hours, take the 20 slowest calls, summarize p95 by target, then select the top three p95 values. — The early top operation still restricts the population to extreme calls and can exclude entire targets. It fits analyzing the retained worst-call subset, not per-target latency across all calls.

Filter six hours, summarize average duration by target, then select the top three averages. — This uses all calls but ranks mean latency rather than p95. Average duration is useful for a mean-performance question, but can conceal tail behavior the requirement explicitly targets.

Filter six hours, summarize p95 by target, then select the top three p95 values. — Compute p95 per target before using top to rank the resulting target summaries. A percentile describes the input distribution presented to the aggregation. Selecting only the slowest individual calls first changes that distribution and can remove targets. The correct order avoids selection bias while keeping the requested percentile and final result limit.

The dependency and request share a trace, but the dependency need not be the request's immediate child. — The join establishes shared trace membership, not necessarily a direct parent-child relationship. Trace identity groups a distributed operation; span identity and parent identity describe its tree. Keeping requestRole and dependencyRole separate also prevents accidentally attributing a downstream call to the request's emitting service merely because they joined.

The dependency is an immediate child of the selected request, regardless of how many services the trace crosses. — Immediate parentage requires the parent-span relationship, not only the shared trace ID. This inference could hold in a trace known to contain only direct child dependencies, but the stem explicitly allows downstream services.

The dependency originated in requestRole, even when dependencyRole has a different value. — cloud_RoleName identifies the emitting service and the query retains the request and dependency values separately. Equating the origins fits same-service dependencies, not a row whose dependencyRole differs.
max(itemCount) — max would show the largest single record weight in each type, useful for inspecting the maximum weight. It does not accumulate the represented volume of all exception records.

sum(itemCount) — Use sum(itemCount), producing represented totals of 30 and 8 for the supplied records. count() answers how many rows survived, not how many events those rows represent. The weighted sum supports a sampling-adjusted estimate; it does not reconstruct every dropped exception or guarantee an exact historical event count.

avg(itemCount) — avg describes the average sampling weight of a retained record. It can characterize weight differences but does not include how many records contribute to each exception type's represented total.

| summarize total = sum(requestCount) by cloud_RoleName — This would aggregate the hourly rows into a total per service and discard time granularity. It suits period totals, not displaying the existing hourly series.
| top 5 by requestCount desc — top selects the five highest-count rows. It suits finding peaks but reduces the result set rather than merely requesting a time-chart display.

| render timechart — Append render timechart. The aggregate defines the data and the render operator defines its requested presentation. A chart cannot repair an incorrect population or grouping, but those are already correct in this stem.

Keep six vaults and reduce total offered secret reads to at most 20,000 per ten seconds. — The offered total is 23,400 reads; the subscription bound is five times the 4,000-per-vault bound, or 20,000 per ten seconds. Both scopes matter. All six individual vaults remain under 4,000, but 6 × 3,900 exceeds 20,000 across the subscription. Splitting the same volume among more vaults in the same scope does not reduce that sum. A design should leave operating headroom; the answer identifies the documented ceiling, not guaranteed latency at the limit.

Split the same read workload evenly across twelve vaults in the same subscription and region. — Additional vaults can distribute a workload that is limited by one vault while the subscription still has headroom. They do not increase this subscription’s aggregate transaction budget.

Consolidate the same read workload into a single vault in the same subscription and region. — A single vault is a valid deployment boundary for a small application. At this offered volume it also exceeds the individual 4,000-read ceiling, so consolidation makes the per-vault constraint worse.

Call get_secret on the original vault and use the returned value. — An authorized get_secret call is appropriate when an application needs a value from an available vault. It neither reads the encrypted backup format nor works around the stipulated original-vault unavailability.

Restore the blob into a vault in the same Azure subscription and geography. — Key Vault backup blobs must be restored into a vault in the same subscription and Azure geography. The service-limits article states that the downloaded backup is encrypted and cannot be decrypted outside Azure. Restoring it within the supported scope is the route to usable data. This is not ordinary get_secret value retrieval or a general cross-subscription migration format.

List the secret’s version properties in the original vault and save that inventory. — Version-property listing supports a metadata audit of an available secret. It does not return secret values or restore the encrypted backup, and it also depends on the original vault here.

Create the async client and credential once for the service, reuse them, and close both asynchronously at shutdown. — Reuse the asynchronous client and credential and close their resources when the application shuts down. The training unit recommends creating the client at application startup and reusing it across requests. It also states that both async client and credential are asynchronous context managers and must be closed when finished. This concerns network-client lifetime, not caching secret values or suppressing permission failures.

Use the synchronous SecretClient for every read and call it directly in the asyncio request handler. — The synchronous SecretClient is appropriate for synchronous application code. Calling it directly in an async request handler does not provide the documented nonblocking vault access.

Create and close a fresh async client and credential for every incoming request. — A scoped async client and credential with cleanup are appropriate for a standalone short-lived operation, as in the unit’s async example. Repeating that setup for every high-throughput request still pays the connection-creation overhead that the documented service-lifetime reuse pattern avoids.

Move the token to a secret value and leave only nonsensitive ownership or rotation labels in tags. — Keep the credential in the protected secret value, not in metadata readable by discovery tools. The storage unit warns that list/get users can read tags and that sensitive data does not belong there. The SDK listing returns properties such as tags and content type without the secret value. Key Vault Reader is deliberately a metadata role; changing value-read permission is not a fix for metadata disclosure.

Move the token from its existing tag into the secret’s content_type property. — content_type is useful as a nonsensitive interpretation hint such as text/plain or application/json. It is part of the listed properties, so relocating a token there does not remove it from the metadata surface.

Keep the token in tags and assign Key Vault Secrets User to the discovery identity. — Secrets User is appropriate for an application that needs actual secret values. Granting that additional access does not redact the existing tag and defeats the discovery-only boundary.

t=225 seconds — An earlier call could qualify with a shorter secret refresh interval that had elapsed by t=225. The configured 300-second interval has not elapsed, regardless of the 60-second ordinary-setting interval.

t=315 seconds — The first call at or after the 300-second secret interval is t=315. The secret interval is independent of the ordinary-setting interval and sentinel changes. It is checked when the application calls refresh(), not by a background timer at exactly t=300. The versionless reference and successful calls are necessary to make this a bounded timing question; it does not promise prompt update if the application stops calling refresh().

Only after the sentinel changes — A sentinel change is the trigger for watched ordinary-setting reloads. Independent secret refresh is specifically provided for secret changes that leave the App Configuration reference and sentinel unchanged.

Reduce refresh_interval to 1 and leave the processing loop unchanged. — A shorter interval can increase checking frequency in an application that already calls refresh regularly. It cannot create calls in this loop.

Call config.refresh() from the processing loop before reading settings. — The application must explicitly call refresh(); the interval is a gate on checks, not an autonomous scheduler. Reading the current Mapping is not the explicit refresh call shown in the provider pattern. With an eligible interval and changed sentinel, the next call can load the new ordinary settings. There is no claim that this makes publication atomic or guarantees completion during an outage.

Add a second WatchKey and leave the processing loop unchanged. — Additional watched keys can signal other ordinary-configuration changes. They do not schedule checks when the application never invokes refresh.

The code argument selects rate-limited sampling at approximately two traces per second. — traces_per_second=2 selects the requested rate-limited policy when overriding sampler environment settings are absent. Those settings are present in this deployment.

The environment selects fixed-percentage sampling at approximately 25 percent of traces. — The configured environment sampler takes precedence and interprets 0.25 as a fraction, not a traces-per-second limit. The export unit explicitly gives sampling environment settings priority over code options. The current configuration document distinguishes fixed-percentage arguments in 0.0–1.0 from rate-limited traces-per-second arguments and places the Python default change at 1.8.6. An explicitly configured sampler does not fall back to the default.

The absence of sampling_ratio in code selects the version’s default rate-limited sampler. — The 1.8.6 default is relevant when neither environment variables nor sampling_ratio/traces_per_second code options configure sampling. This deployment supplies both forms, so absence of one code parameter does not activate that default.

Inner-join the raw tables on operation_Id, then use count() to count the joined rows per trace. — Counting the raw join is appropriate for counting matched request/dependency pairs; here it returns six, not the two independent input counts.

Summarize count() by cloud_RoleName separately in each table, then inner-join on cloud_RoleName. — Grouping by cloud role supports independent per-service request and dependency totals. It combines different traces emitted by that service and cannot provide the stipulated one-row-per-operation_Id result.

Summarize count() by operation_Id separately in each table, then inner-join the two summaries. — Aggregate each input to one row per trace before joining so neither input’s rows multiply the other’s count. An inner join on a key with two request rows and three dependency rows produces six matching pairs. Those are not two independent telemetry counts. Each per-trace summary has a unique key, so their join carries the separately computed 2 and 3. The inner join deliberately excludes traces missing from either table; an outer-join requirement is not implied.
